result: The TREM2 ectodomain crystal structure was determined at 3.1 Å resolution, revealing a V-type Ig domain with nine β-strands, two short α-helix passages, two disulfide bonds (C36-C110 and C51-C60), and a single N-acetylglucosamine glycan at N79. The asymmetric unit contains two structurally similar monomers (Cα RMSD 0.65 Å) with high-quality refinement statistics (97.7% favored Ramachandran, 0% outliers, MolProbity score 1.66).
evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C10, C79-C83 collectively provide comprehensive structural characterization with crystallographic data, electron density maps, and quality metrics. The resolution determination methodology (Table 1) and refinement statistics (Table 2) support the structural claims. The electron density for key features (NAG, disulfides) is shown in figures.

result: NHD mutations (Y38C, T66M, V126G) are buried within the TREM2 core structure with low solvent accessibility. Structural analysis predicts these mutations disrupt protein folding through mechanisms including interference with disulfide bond formation (Y38C), steric disruption of core packing (T66M), and destabilization of hydrophobic cores (V126G). Y38 and V126 are conserved within the TREM family, while T66 is conserved specifically in TREM2 across species.
evaluation: Claims C2, C11-C17 are supported by crystal structure analysis showing buried positions (Figure 1c solvent accessibility data), detailed structural contacts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and sequence conservation analysis (Figure 5c). The mechanistic predictions are reasonable inferences from structural data, though experimental validation of folding disruption is provided separately in other results.

result: AD risk variants (R47H, R62H, N68K, D87N, T96K) are located on the TREM2 protein surface with high solvent accessibility. R47 is well-ordered with its side chain lying parallel to the surface and engaging T66. R62, N68, D87, and T96 are surface-exposed with varying degrees of intramolecular contacts.
evaluation: Claims C3, C18, C20-C22 are directly supported by crystal structure analysis with quantitative solvent accessibility measurements (Figure 1c) and electron density maps (Figure 1e-g). The structural positions and contacts are clearly documented in the figures and supplementary structural analysis.

result: WT and AD risk variant TREM2 ectodomains elute as monomers in size exclusion chromatography and migrate as monomers under non-reducing conditions. In contrast, NHD mutants (Y38C, T66M, V126G) elute earlier consistent with aggregation and form covalent dimers/trimers under non-reducing conditions, indicating aberrant intermolecular disulfide bond formation.
evaluation: Claims C23-C27 are supported by SEC chromatography data (Figure 2a, Figure 2—figure supplement 1) and SDS-PAGE analysis (Figure 2b-c). The differential behavior between AD variants and NHD mutants is clearly demonstrated across multiple independent experiments with consistent results.

result: NHD mutants show decreased anti-TREM2 antibody staining but normal anti-FLAG staining in surface expression assays, despite slightly higher whole-cell expression levels. The Y38C mutant displays diffuse intracellular accumulation in permeabilized cells versus punctate staining for WT and R47H. NHD mutants form SDS-resistant aggregates when expressed as full-length proteins in 293T cells.
evaluation: Claims C28-C31, C84 are supported by flow cytometry (Figure 2d-e), confocal microscopy (Figure 2g), western blot (Figure 2f, 2h), and commercial antibody validation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The differential recognition by conformational versus non-conformational antibodies provides strong evidence for misfolding. Multiple independent assays converge on the same conclusion.

result: Both Y38C and R47H TREM2 variants show some signaling potential but neither sustains ERK phosphorylation as efficiently as WT TREM2 in RAW264.7 and Cos-7 cells following anti-FLAG crosslinking.
evaluation: Claim C32 is supported by phospho-ERK immunoblot data in two cell types (Figure 2i-j). The experiments show initial signaling at 10 minutes but loss of sustained signaling at 30 minutes for both variants compared to WT. However, the mechanistic interpretation requires caution as multiple factors could explain reduced sustained signaling.

result: R47H shows a subtle but statistically significant conformational change by CD spectroscopy (altered 214/233 nm ratio), while R62H and T96K do not. All AD variants show slightly reduced thermal stability by DSF and chemical denaturation, with T96K showing the most pronounced destabilization. All variants show reversible thermal denaturation that is abolished by DTT.
evaluation: Claims C33-C38 are supported by CD spectroscopy (Figure 3a-b), DSF (Figure 3c), thermal denaturation CD (Figure 3d), and GuHCl denaturation experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b). Statistical analysis confirms significance for R47H CD differences. The effects are subtle but reproducible across multiple protein preparations and complementary techniques.

result: TREM2 shows only broad discrimination for anionic phospholipids (PA, PG, PI, PS) over neutral lipids (PC, PE) in direct binding assays, with no differences observed between WT and AD variant ectodomains. TREM2-lipid binding is not sensitive to EDTA, unlike TIM and CD300 proteins, indicating a different binding mechanism.
evaluation: Claims C39, C62, C63 are supported by phospholipid ELISA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a-b), liposome sedimentation assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c), and EDTA sensitivity experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e-f). The lack of selectivity and calcium-independence distinguishes TREM2 from other phospholipid-binding Ig domains. However, the negative result (no variant differences) should be interpreted cautiously.

result: TREM2/SA-PE tetramers bind to N2A and THP-1 cells, with binding dramatically decreased by PMA/ionomycin treatment. TREM2 binding is sensitive to proteinase treatment (abolished by proteinase K, reduced by chymotrypsin and elastase) without affecting cell viability (>99%), demonstrating that TREM2-L contains a protein component.
evaluation: Claims C40-C45 are supported by flow cytometry experiments (Figure 4b-d, Figure 4—figure supplement 2a-b,f) showing specific binding that is modulated by cellular stimulation and protease treatment. The viability control (C44) validates that protease effects are not due to cell death. The inference that TREM2-L contains protein (C45) is reasonable but does not exclude additional components.

result: TREM2 tetramer binding is GAG-dependent, observed in CHO-K1 cells but not GAG-deficient CHO-745 cells. Treatment with heparinases had pronounced effects on TREM2 binding to CHO, THP-1, and N2A cells, while chondroitinase had minimal effect, implicating heparan sulfate as a major component of cell surface TREM2-L.
evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are supported by flow cytometry experiments using GAG-deficient cells (Figure 4e) and enzymatic GAG removal (Figure 4e-g). The differential sensitivity to heparinases versus chondroitinase across multiple cell types provides strong evidence for heparan sulfate involvement. The CHO-745 control is well-established in the literature (cited).

result: The R47H variant shows markedly diminished binding to N2A and THP-1 cells, while T96K significantly increases binding. R62H shows intermediate reduction in binding, with effects varying by assay format (more pronounced in anti-6H format, less dramatic in competition or tetramer staining).
evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are supported by multiple binding assay formats: tetramer staining (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c-d), anti-6His detection (Figure 4k-l), and competition assays (Figure 4—figure supplement 2e). The convergence of results across different formats strengthens the conclusions, though the assay-dependent differences for R62H suggest intermediate affinity changes that are near detection limits for some methods.

result: TREM2 has a large basic surface patch not present in other TREM family receptors (mTREM1, hTREM1, TLT-1). The residues constituting this basic patch are highly conserved within TREM2 but not in the rest of the TREM family. TREM2 tetramers bind N2A cells while TREML2 and TREML4 tetramers do not. The T96K mutation extends this basic patch, explaining its gain-of-function. Mutations R76D and R77D within this patch decrease binding similarly to validated AD risk variants.
evaluation: Claims C51-C55, C92 are supported by electrostatic surface analysis (Figure 5a-f), sequence alignment (Figure 5c), comparative binding experiments with TREM family members (Figure 4i), and mutagenesis of basic patch residues (Figure 5g). The convergence of structural, evolutionary, and functional data strongly supports the identification of a TREM2-specific functional surface. The gain-of-function explanation for T96K is structurally reasonable.

result: NHD-linked mutant residues are buried and impact protein folding and stability, while AD-linked variant residues are on the protein surface and do not diminish stability or surface expression but instead impact ligand engagement.
evaluation: Claims C56-C57 synthesize multiple lines of evidence from structural analysis (C2-C3), biophysical characterization (C33-C38), surface expression studies (C28-C31), and ligand binding assays (C48-C50). The dichotomy between NHD and AD mutations is consistently supported across all experimental approaches. This represents a well-supported mechanistic model integrating the entire dataset.

result: TREM2 has a long narrow hydrophobic patch on the end most distal from the plasma membrane that is the most likely lipid-binding surface. This hydrophobic patch is adjacent to the basic patch, which could mediate interaction with anionic phospholipid head groups.
evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are based on structural analysis of surface properties (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) but represent inferences without direct experimental validation. While the structural observations are sound, the functional assignment as the lipid-binding surface is speculative. The direct lipid binding experiments (C39, C62) did not test this hypothesis specifically, and the proposed mechanism differs from the discussion of GAG-mediated clustering (C66).

result: TREM2 interaction with GAGs in cis is likely required to orient or cluster TREM2 to mediate signaling upon phospholipid stimulation. Alternatively, phospholipids may function to orient TREM2 for proper presentation to GAGs and/or additional protein surface receptors.
evaluation: Claims C66-C67 represent mechanistic hypotheses to reconcile observations that R47H binds phospholipids directly but doesn't signal in cellular assays (cited Wang et al., 2015) with the finding that R47H has reduced GAG binding. While the reasoning is logical, these are speculative models without direct experimental validation. C67 is explicitly marked as speculation in the evidence. Additional experiments would be needed to distinguish between these models.

result: Prior genetic and clinical studies establish that TREM2 R47H is associated with AD risk similar to APOE4, correlates with increased CSF tau, and has been identified in FTD, PD, and ALS patients. R62H is associated with increased AD risk in independent studies. Homozygous TREM2 mutations cause NHD or frontotemporal dementia, while AD-associated mutations are heterozygous. N68K, D87N, and T96K associations with AD remain uncertain due to rarity.
evaluation: Claims C4, C68-C69, C74-C78 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations. The claims correctly distinguish between well-validated associations (R47H, R62H) and uncertain associations (N68K, D87N, T96K) based on statistical power. The genetic inheritance patterns (homozygous NHD vs. heterozygous AD) are well-established. These claims provide essential context but represent prior work rather than new findings.

result: TREM2 is an innate immune receptor expressed on multiple myeloid cell types with a type I receptor structure consisting of an extracellular V-type Ig domain, stalk, transmembrane domain associating with DAP12, and cytoplasmic tail. TREM2 has been shown to play anti-inflammatory roles in vitro but can also promote inflammatory disease in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C5-C6, C71-C73 accurately summarize established knowledge about TREM2 with appropriate citations. The structural description (C6) is consistent with the crystal structure determined in this study. These claims provide necessary background but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings from this manuscript.

result: TREM2-deficient AD mouse models display fewer activated microglia, with TREM2 absence preventing microglia proliferation and promoting apoptosis, correlated with increased Aβ plaque accumulation. Microglia display less activation and do not engulf Aβ plaques, promoting diffuse neurotoxic Aβ structures.
evaluation: Claims C58-C61, C87 accurately cite prior mouse model studies (Wang et al., 2015; Jay et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016; Yuan et al., 2016). These findings provide important biological context for interpreting the structural and functional studies but represent prior work. The citations are appropriate and the summaries are accurate.

result: Rare AD cases with heterozygous NHD variants (Q33X, Y38C, T66M) have been reported. Soluble TREM2 may be a survival signal in bone-marrow macrophages and can be detected in the CNS. Some AD risk variants, but not NHD mutant proteins, are readily detected in patient CSF.
evaluation: Claims C85-C86, C88-C89 cite prior work including the authors' own studies (Wu et al., 2015; Piccio et al., 2016; Guerreiro et al., 2013b). These observations support the dosage hypothesis discussed in the manuscript. The claims are accurately cited and provide relevant context for the discussion.

result: A concurrent study reported that TREM2 binds lipid-loaded ApoE, facilitating uptake of Aβ-loaded lipoparticles by microglia, and suggests AD risk variants decrease ApoE binding, though binding affinities were not quantitated.
evaluation: Claims C90-C91 accurately cite a concurrent study (Yeh et al., 2016) published during manuscript preparation. The authors appropriately note limitations of the cited work (lack of quantitation) and discuss how it relates to their findings. This represents accurate citation of concurrent work rather than new findings.
